medium.resumo: How Anthropic redesigned source control to keep pace with AI-driven software development.
medium.conteudo_html:
How Anthropic redesigned source control to keep pace with AI-driven software development.

AI coding agents are changing how software is built. But as code generation accelerates, a new challenge emerges: can the infrastructure around software development keep up?

Anthropic’s answer is Scion, an internal source control system designed to handle the growing volume of AI-generated code.

The Problem: Code Generation Is No Longer the Bottleneck

Anthropic reported that its daily merged code changes increased from approximately 2,500 in May 2026 to more than 30,000 in September — over a 10× increase in four months.

Traditional Git-based infrastructure began struggling with this scale. Repository mirrors, checkouts, and CI workloads introduced overhead that became increasingly expensive to manage.

The lesson is straightforward: making code generation faster is not enough. The systems responsible for testing, reviewing, and integrating that code must evolve too.

What Is Scion?

Scion is Anthropic’s approach to source control at AI scale. Rather than relying on every client maintaining a substantial local repository, it moves more operations to centralized services.

Its design focuses on several principles:

  • Server-side operations: Commits, merges, and history queries are handled centrally.
  • Efficient caching: Multiple cache layers reduce repeated data retrieval.
  • Incremental changes: Operations focus on what changed rather than repeatedly processing the entire repository.
  • Lightweight checkouts: CI jobs and agents can access only the files they need.
  • Horizontal scalability: Infrastructure components can scale as workloads increase.

The result is a source control architecture designed around highly concurrent, always-connected AI agents rather than primarily human-paced development.

The Reported Results

According to Anthropic, Scion delivered significant improvements:

  • 200× smaller infrastructure footprint in CPU and memory requirements compared with its previous Git-mirroring infrastructure.
  • Up to 100× faster checkouts for CI and research workloads.
  • 25% CPU capacity savings in CI.

These are results from Anthropic’s own environment, not independent benchmarks. Nevertheless, they illustrate how infrastructure redesign can produce gains beyond those achieved by improving the AI models themselves.

Better Code Is Only Half the Problem

I once watched Matt Pocock discuss how to improve AI-generated code by slowing the agent down and using test-driven development (TDD). The idea is to give the agent tighter feedback loops: write a test, implement the behavior, verify the result, and repeat. This helps the agent produce more reliable code instead of generating a large implementation in one pass.

But it raises another question.

Even if we slow down individual agents, what happens when many agents are generating code in parallel?

Better feedback loops can improve code quality, but they do not necessarily reduce the total volume of code entering a system. In fact, when agents become more reliable and easier to scale, teams may run more of them concurrently.

This creates a second challenge: beyond improving the quality of generated code, we need to manage its volume, review burden, integration cost, and long-term maintenance and infrastructure resillience.

Anthropic’s Scion story illustrates why this matters. The challenge is no longer just helping AI write better code. It is building engineering infrastructure capable of handling the scale at which that code is produced.

Why This Matters for MLOps and AI Engineering

Scion highlights a challenge that extends beyond source control.

As AI accelerates development, bottlenecks can move to testing, deployment, observability, and infrastructure management. MLOps teams face a similar pattern when automated experimentation and model development increase the volume of workloads that pipelines must handle.

Three lessons stand out:

1. Design for concurrency, not just speed.

AI agents can execute many tasks in parallel. Systems need to handle concurrent workloads without introducing excessive contention, locking, or resource duplication.

2. Optimize the entire lifecycle.

Faster code generation provides limited value if testing, integration, and deployment remain slow. Performance improvements should target the complete workflow, not just one stage.

3. Reconsider established architectural assumptions.

Git remains suitable for most development teams, and Scion is not intended as a universal replacement. Its broader significance is that AI-driven workloads may justify different architectural choices when existing infrastructure reaches its limits.

Scion is a useful example of a broader shift in AI engineering: infrastructure is becoming a critical part of scaling AI productivity.

The next challenge is not simply building agents that can write more code. It is building systems that can reliably test, integrate, and manage the output of those agents at scale.

As AI makes production faster, the surrounding infrastructure becomes an increasingly important competitive advantage.

Source: Anthropic Engineering — Redesigning Source Control

medium.titulo: Custom Tools for LangChain and CrewAI: Wrapping Proxy Rotation into Agentic Workflows
medium.resumo: In the current era of AI development, we have largely moved past the “Chatbot” phase and entered the “Agent” phase. We are no longer…
medium.conteudo_html:
In the current era of AI development, we have largely moved past the “Chatbot” phase and entered the “Agent” phase. We are no longer impressed by an LLM that can write a poem; we want an agent that can conduct market research, monitor competitors, and aggregate data autonomously. However, there is a silent wall that most developers hit the moment their agents leave the local sandbox and enter the open web: Anti-bot detection.

If you are building with LangChain or CrewAI, you’ve likely realized that an agent is only as good as its tools. If your SearchTool or ScrapingTool gets blocked after three requests because of a flagged IP, your expensive multi-agent system becomes a collection of very polite "I'm sorry, I can't access that" messages.

This guide explores the senior-level architecture of wrapping proxy rotation into custom tools, ensuring your agents possess the digital “stealth” required for high-stakes data acquisition.

Why Do Agents Fail at Scale? The Invisible Infrastructure Gap

Every senior engineer knows that the difference between a prototype and a production system is how it handles failure. When an agent fails to fetch a URL, the LLM often tries to “hallucinate” the content or loops infinitely trying to fix a problem it doesn’t understand.

The bottleneck isn’t the LLM’s reasoning — it’s the network identity. Websites today use sophisticated fingerprinting. If your agent makes twenty concurrent requests from a single AWS Lambda IP, it’s not just the request that dies; your agent’s “chain of thought” breaks. To build resilient agents, we must treat proxy management not as a peripheral networking task, but as a core capability of the agent’s toolkit.

How Does Proxy Rotation Integrate with LangChain and CrewAI?

To the agent, a tool is a black box. The agent provides an input (a URL or a search query) and expects a clean string of data in return. Our job is to build a “Smart Tool” that manages the following under the hood:

  1. IP Rotation: Switching exit nodes for every request.
  2. Header Management: Mimicking real browser headers (User-Agents).
  3. Session Persistence: Optionally keeping the same IP for a “multi-step” scraping task.
  4. Error Handling: Retrying with a new proxy if a 403 or 429 status code is returned.

In LangChain, this is handled via the @tool decorator or by subclassing BaseTool. In CrewAI, we leverage these LangChain tools to give our "Research Analyst" or "Data Specialist" agents their "eyes."

The Architecture: Designing the RotatedProxySearchTool

Let’s look at a robust implementation strategy. We won’t just use a simple requests.get(). We will build a class-based tool that integrates with a proxy provider (like Bright Data, Smartproxy, or Oxylabs) using their backconnect entry points.

1. The Core Logic (The “Fridge” Ingredients)

We need a way to format our proxy credentials and inject them into the request lifecycle.

import requests
from langchain.tools import tool
from typing import Optional, Dict

class ProxyManager:
    def __init__(self, proxy_url: str):
        self.proxy_url = proxy_url

    def get_html(self, target_url: str, headers: Optional[Dict] = None):
        proxies = {
            "http": self.proxy_url,
            "https": self.proxy_url,
        }
        try:
            response = requests.get(
                target_url, 
                proxies=proxies, 
                headers=headers, 
                timeout=15
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.text
        except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
            return f"Error: The request failed due to {str(e)}"

2. Wrapping for LangChain/CrewAI

The agent needs to know when and how to use this. This requires a clear docstring, as the LLM uses the docstring to understand the tool’s utility.

@tool("stealth_web_scraper")
def stealth_web_scraper(url: str) -> str:
    """
    Useful for scraping websites that have strict bot protections. 
    This tool uses a rotated proxy pool to hide the agent's identity.
    Input should be a full URL.
    """
    # In a real scenario, these would be env variables
    PROXY_USER = "your_username"
    PROXY_PASS = "your_password"
    PROXY_HOST = "zproxy.lum-superproxy.io:22225" # Example backconnect
    
    proxy_uri = f"http://{PROXY_USER}:{PROXY_PASS}@{PROXY_HOST}"
    
    manager = ProxyManager(proxy_uri)
    
    # Advanced: Rotate User-Agents to match the proxy rotation
    headers = {
        "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36..."
    }
    
    return manager.get_html(url, headers=headers)

The Resilience Framework: Strategies for Senior Implementations

Building the tool is only 20% of the work. The other 80% is ensuring it doesn’t break your agent’s budget or logic.

A. The “Backconnect” Advantage

Instead of managing a list of thousands of IPs in your code, use a Backconnect Proxy. This provides you with a single entry point (e.g., proxy.provider.com:8000). The provider handles the rotation on their end every time you send a request. This keeps your tool code clean and offloads the heavy lifting.

B. Sticky Sessions vs. Pure Rotation

  • Pure Rotation: Every request gets a new IP. Best for broad scraping (e.g., “Find the price of X on 50 different sites”).
  • Sticky Sessions: You use a session ID in your proxy string (e.g., user-session-123). This keeps the same IP for a period. This is vital if your agent needs to "Login" or "Add to Cart"—actions where a changing IP would trigger a security alert.

C. Smart Retries and LLM Logic

If a proxy fails, don’t just return an error to the agent immediately. Implement a “Retry with new IP” logic within the tool. However, if the site is genuinely down, the tool should report that so the agent can pivot its strategy.

Step-by-Step Guide: Deploying Proxy Tools in CrewAI

If you are using CrewAI, the integration is seamless because CrewAI is built on top of LangChain’s tool specifications.

  1. Define the Tool: Use the code structure provided above.
  2. Assign to Agent:
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew

researcher = Agent(
  role='Senior Web Researcher',
  goal='Extract deep market insights from competitor websites',
  backstory='Expert in navigating complex web structures and bypassing restrictions.',
  tools=[stealth_web_scraper],
  verbose=True
)

3. Monitor the Logs: Watch how the agent handles 403 errors. A well-wrapped tool will abstract the “proxy struggle” away, leaving the agent to focus on data synthesis.

Final Thoughts: The Ethical and Technical Frontier

As we move toward more autonomous systems, the “Network Identity” of our agents becomes a critical architectural pillar. Wrapping proxy rotation into custom tools isn’t just about bypassing blocks; it’s about building reliability.

A senior developer understands that an agent is a guest on the web. Using proxies responsibly — respecting robots.txt where possible while ensuring your system doesn't collapse under the weight of a single IP ban—is the mark of a professional AI implementation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Decouple logic: Keep your proxy rotation logic in a manager class, separate from the agent’s tool definition.
  • Backconnect is king: Don’t manage IP lists manually; use provider-side rotation.
  • Context matters: Use sticky sessions for stateful interactions and pure rotation for stateless data gathering.

The next time you build a LangChain or CrewAI workflow, ask yourself: Is my agent resilient enough to survive the open web? If the answer involves a single static IP, it’s time to wrap your tools in a new layer of digital camouflage.

medium.titulo: I kept losing my Claude artifacts, so I made a mod
medium.resumo: A lot of what I make with Claude now ends up as an artifact: a page or a doc that lives on claude.ai instead of in the chat. That includes…
medium.conteudo_html:
A lot of what I make with Claude now ends up as an artifact: a page or a doc that lives on claude.ai instead of in the chat. That includes quotes for Aori Creative clients, a pricing sheet, a security overview of my CMS, a script for a YouTube video I’m planning and notes on a side project’s recommendation algorithm. They’re useful, and I come back to them.

Or I try to. Finding them again was the hard part.

A gallery that only grows

Artifacts land in one long list, newest first. That’s fine for the first few. For me, after a couple of weeks, a client quote sat next to a video script, which sat next to an internal security note, and half the titles only made sense on the day I made them.

The chat a page came from was usually closed by then, so there was no easy way back to it. I’d scroll, open the wrong one, scroll again, and sometimes just ask Claude to make the thing again.

First, some order

The quick fix was to tidy what I already had:

  • Categories in the title. Every artifact got a short prefix: company, clients, YouTube or side projects. The gallery is still one list, but now I can scan it.
  • A catalogue in Notion. One database with the title, category, a one-line summary and a link. That’s where I go when I want to search or sort.
  • An index page. One more artifact, pinned to the sidebar, that lists everything by category with a search box. Its entries live in the artifact’s own small database, so adding an entry doesn’t mean republishing the page.

That cleaned up the past. But it only stays clean if every new artifact gets filed too, and I knew I’d forget.

Then, a mod that asks at the right moment

Claude Code lets you write mods: small modules that hook into what Claude does and can draw a little UI next to the prompt. That was the right place for this. The moment to file an artifact is right after it’s made, while I still remember what it’s for.

So now, when Claude publishes a new artifact, a row appears above the prompt once Claude is done:

New artifact “Q3 pricing review” — add it to your catalogue? [Add] [Skip]

Press Add, and Claude picks a category from my list, writes a one-line summary, adds it to the Notion database and the index page, and renames it with the category prefix. Press Skip, and the row goes away.

A few details mattered more than I expected:

  • It only asks about new artifacts. Updating a page or fixing a typo doesn’t count, and the index page never asks to file itself.
  • It waits. The row only shows up when Claude isn’t busy, so it never interrupts a task halfway through.
  • It speaks my language. My copy asks in Traditional Chinese, and it also comes in English, Simplified Chinese, Japanese and Korean.

Sharing it

Once it worked for me, it seemed silly to keep it to myself. So I made it generic: Notion is optional, the categories are yours, and there’s an index page template you can publish as is. It’s open source on GitHub, and installing it is one line at the Claude Code prompt:

/plugin install artifact-catalog --marketplace amsyeung/artifact-catalog

Leave everything empty, and the first time you press Add, Claude will ask where you’d like things filed.

What changed

  • I find things again. Pinned index, by category, with search. No more scrolling.
  • Nothing piles up. Filing takes one press, at the moment I still remember what the artifact is for.
  • The titles make sense. Even in the plain gallery list.

It’s a small tool for a small annoyance. But I use Claude every day, and this was the kind of friction that adds up. Small fixes like this are often the ones I end up using the most.

medium.titulo: Why Your Game Site Feels Laggy: Debugging a Main Thread Contention Problem
medium.resumo: Users waited 1.8 seconds after clicking “Start” before seeing anything. I thought the iframe was slow to load. It turned out the main…
medium.conteudo_html:
Users waited 1.8 seconds after clicking “Start” before seeing anything. I thought the iframe was slow to load. It turned out the main thread was being crushed by a crowd of “reasonable” tasks.

A few months ago, I was building a small game collection site (playfiddlebops.com). The list page and detail pages ran smoothly, but after users clicked “Start Game,” the page would freeze for about 1.8 seconds. The button had no hover feedback, no click ripple — it felt like it had crashed.
My first instinct was straightforward: the iframe must be slow to load game assets.
That instinct was wrong. And the first optimization I made based on that instinct actually made things worse.
Here’s how I found the real cause and brought INP (Interaction to Next Paint) down from 480ms to 120ms.

Environment

Test devices were a Moto G Power (Android 13, Chrome 125) and an iPhone 12 (iOS 17.4 Safari). Network was throttled to 4G in Chrome DevTools, 20ms RTT. Tools were the DevTools Performance panel and Lighthouse 12.

First Attempt: I Blamed the iframe

I added loading="lazy" to the iframe and delayed setting the src until after the user clicked. The logic sounded reasonable - don’t load game assets until the user clicks.
The result was slower after the click.
Because the game assets could have been loaded earlier, and I pushed that to after the click, the user had to wait through a full load cycle. First attempt failed. The problem wasn’t the iframe’s load timing.

Recording the Full Timeline in the Performance Panel

I recorded a full “page load → click start → game appears” timeline again, and found the key information.
Within the 1.8 seconds after the click event fired, the main thread ran these tasks in sequence:

  • React hydration cleanup: ~42ms
  • Ad SDK initialization: ~38ms
  • Analytics script execution: ~21ms
  • Thumbnail processing (createImageBitmap): ~47ms
  • Game SDK initialization: ~55ms
  • WebGL context creation and shader compilation: ~63ms
    None of these tasks looked catastrophic on its own, but they ran almost back-to-back on the timeline. The total was around 266ms, plus the browser’s own rendering, style calculation, and layout overhead, which showed up as 480ms INP.
    This matches what the OzoGames developer summarized from practice: performance problems usually aren’t caused by one obviously bad script. They come from too many reasonable tasks trying to run at the same time. The browser doesn’t care whether each individual task has a reason to exist. If enough work arrives on the main thread at once, players still feel a slow page.

The Key Insight: The Main Thread Is a Shared Resource

There was a shift in perspective here that I only really understood later.
JavaScript execution, layout, style calculation, event handling, and many rendering tasks all depend on the browser’s main thread. Imagine the page loading while doing all of these at once: React hydration, analytics initialization, ad initialization, consent management, recommendation rendering, thumbnail processing, game iframe initialization, game SDK initialization, WebGL startup.
On their own, none of these tasks may be catastrophic. The problem is that the browser receives all of them in the same short window, causing contention.
The way to think about browser performance shouldn’t just be “how expensive is this script” — it should be “what else is happening when this script runs.” Timing matters almost as much as size.

The Fix: Priority Scheduling + yield

Five-Level Priority Model

Based on the diagnosis, I designed a priority model:

  • Priority 1: Critical rendering and interaction (page shell, button response)
  • Priority 2: Business-critical initialization (user auth, core state)
  • Priority 3: Visible secondary UI (thumbnails, recommendation areas)
  • Priority 4: Non-critical analytics and enhancements (analytics scripts, consent management)
  • Priority 5: Heavy features triggered by user intent (game runtime)
    For a game page, the game runtime itself belongs to Priority 5 until the player presses Play.

Splitting Long Tasks with yield

The fix wasn’t “delete tasks” — it was “move tasks,” changing when they run.
The core technique is yield: periodically give the main thread back to the browser inside a long task, so higher-priority work like user input can run.
setTimeout can also yield, but it has a problem: the continuation after the yield goes to the end of the task queue. Any other task scheduled in the meantime - a third-party analytics callback, another component’s task, another setTimeout - runs before you regain control. Your loop can get stuck behind work you don’t care about, and a task that should finish in 100ms can stretch unpredictably.
scheduler.yield() solves this. It returns a Promise, execution pauses at the await, and the main thread is handed back. The key difference: the continuation goes into a priority queue. When the browser comes back, your function resumes before other similar waiting tasks, not after them.
In Chrome’s framework, the continuation of scheduler.yield() has higher priority than same-level scheduler.postTask() tasks, which prevents your loop from starving.
The rewritten loop barely changes:

async function processThumbnails(thumbnails) {
 for (const [i, thumb] of thumbnails.entries()) {
 await createImageBitmap(thumb)
 if (i % 10 === 0) {
 await scheduler.yield()
 }
 }
}

Concrete Scheduling Changes

Defer ad and analytics scripts until after the page is interactive.

<head>
 <script src="/app.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
 <script>
 const loadThirdParty = () => {
 const scripts = [
 'https://analytics.example.com/tracker.js',
 'https://ads.example.com/loader.js',
 ]
 scripts.forEach(src => {
 const s = document.createElement('script')
 s.src = src
 s.async = true
 document.body.appendChild(s)
 })
 }
 ['click', 'scroll', 'keydown'].forEach(evt =>
 addEventListener(evt, loadThirdParty, { once: true })
 )
 setTimeout(loadThirdParty, 3000)
 </script>
</body>

Process thumbnails in chunks. Instead of processing all thumbnails at once, yield every 10.
Delay game iframe initialization until after the user clicks. This was already implemented with the facade pattern in the previous article. The key point: game runtime initialization (WebGL context creation, shader compilation) is moved to Priority 5 and only triggered after the user clicks.

Safari Compatibility

scheduler.yield() is stable in Chrome and Edge (129+, September 2024), covering about 70% of global traffic, but Safari and Firefox don’t support it yet. A feature detection and fallback is needed:

function yieldToMain() {
 if (globalThis.scheduler?.yield) {
 return scheduler.yield()
 }
 return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
}

The fallback uses setTimeout(0). The continuation still goes to the end of the queue, but at least it doesn’t throw.

Verification Data

After the fix, I tested 10 times each on a Moto G Power (Chrome 125, 4G throttling, 20ms RTT), median:

  • INP (click start): 480ms before, 120ms after
  • First Contentful Paint (FCP): 1.4s, unchanged
  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): 2.1s, unchanged
  • First-load JS (gzip): 85KB → 103KB
  • Main thread long tasks (2s after click): 6 → 2
    FCP and LCP didn’t change, because those metrics measure when page content first appears, and the post-click performance problem doesn’t affect them. INP is the correct metric for interaction responsiveness.
    （When publishing to Medium, turn this section into a comparison image, since Medium doesn’t handle Markdown tables well.）

Trade-offs

First-load JS grew by about 18KB. Because of the scheduler.yield() compatibility code and task scheduling logic. This is a conscious trade-off: 18KB for INP dropping from 480ms to 120ms.
Task scheduling complexity increased. Tasks that used to run synchronously now need to be split and queued, reducing code readability. Every task that needs to yield has to consider “where to yield” and “whether the continuation after yielding is safe.”
Safari isn’t fully optimized. The fallback uses setTimeout(0), and the continuation goes to the end of the task queue. The improvement on Safari is smaller than on Chrome. Measured Safari INP is about 220ms, worse than Chrome’s 120ms, but much better than 480ms before the optimization.

Unresolved

  • Occasional white screen on iOS Safari: On low-end iPhones, game iframe initialization still occasionally produces a white screen. Currently falls back to retrying up to 3 times after the click.
  • Precompiling WebGL shaders: If there were a way to precompile shaders before the user clicks without creating a rendering context, the post-click delay could be reduced further. No reliable cross-browser solution found yet.
  • Third-party script main thread usage can’t be fully controlled: The initialization timing of analytics scripts and ad SDKs can be deferred, but their main thread usage during execution can’t be split, because it’s third-party code.

What This Means for You

If you’re building a game site, or any site that embeds heavy interactive components, here’s my advice:
Don’t just look at individual script duration. The real problem is often tasks crowding into the same time window. Record a full timeline in the Performance panel and look at “who’s competing with whom,” not “who’s slowest.”
Prioritization is more realistic than deletion. You can’t delete ads, analytics, or thumbnails. But you can decide when they run.
INP is the right metric for interaction. No matter how good FCP and LCP look, if users wait 1.8 seconds after clicking, the experience is bad.

References

  • Chrome for Developers’ scheduler.yield() documentation explains the mechanism and continuation priority in detail
  • DEV community articles on INP optimization show the problems with setTimeoutyielding and the improvements in scheduler.yield()
  • The OzoGames developer’s practical summary provides the “main thread is a shared resource” and five-level priority model framework

This article is based on my own project debugging notes. AI was used only for grammar checking and structural suggestions; the technical judgments and test data come from actual runs.

medium.titulo: Next.js vs Vue.js: Which Is Better for Frontend Development in 2026?
medium.resumo: Next.js and Vue.js are popular technologies for building modern websites, but they have different features and development approaches.
medium.conteudo_html:
Next.js and Vue.js are popular technologies for building modern websites, but they have different features and development approaches.

Next.js is a React-based framework that supports server-side rendering, static generation, and full-stack development. It is suitable for complex websites, e-commerce platforms, and applications that need flexible rendering options.

Vue.js is a JavaScript framework known for its simple syntax, flexibility, and beginner-friendly learning experience. It is useful for creating interactive interfaces and responsive websites.

Both technologies can deliver excellent performance when developed properly. Next.js is a good choice for developers working with React, while Vue.js is ideal for those who prefer a straightforward approach to frontend development.

Final Verdict: Choose Next.js for React-based applications and advanced framework features. Choose Vue.js for simplicity, flexibility, and an approachable learning experience.

Nem sempre os influenciadores são notícia por maus exemplos. Hoje, trazemos dois casos de atletas que estão usando a sua influência para o bem. A Thalya Hill fez um alerta importante sobre as regras de antidoping, enquanto o holandês Matty VV mostrou a importância da honestidade ao corrigir seu tempo no Strava após uma maratona.

Antidoping não é só para a elite

A corredora e influenciadora Thalya Hill desmontou um mito comum entre os amadores: o de que as regras antidoping só se aplicam a atletas profissionais. Em um vídeo, ela contou que, mesmo sendo amadora, foi selecionada para um teste antidoping após vencer uma prova. O resultado dela foi negativo, mas ela soube que outros corredores amadores, que apenas participaram do evento, foram testados, falharam e acabaram suspensos.

Thalya reforçou que todo corredor deve se informar sobre as regras e a lista de substâncias proibidas no site da Autoridade Brasileira de Controle de Dopagem (ABCD), já que nem tudo que é vendido em farmácias é permitido. Ela também mencionou as regras sobre o uso de celulares e fones, que são proibidos para quem disputa na categoria competitiva, mas liberados para a participativa.
